procedural_history.impugned_order: Final Judgment and Order dated 20.10.2010 in Crl. A. No.1952/2005 passed by the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State of Karnataka filed Criminal Appeal No.1952 of 2005 before the High Court, aggrieved by the Judgment and Order dated 09.06.2005 (likely an acquittal) from the Trial Court. The High Court allowed the appeal filed by the State against the appellant, reversing the order of acquittal passed by the Trial Court. The appeal against the co-accused was dismissed.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, aggrieved by the High Court's judgment of conviction and sentence, filed a criminal appeal (No. 859 of 2011) before the Supreme Court under The Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and discharged the appellant from bail.

directions: The appellant is discharged from the liability of his bail bonds.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal order passed by the Trial Court, which was based on the finding that the prosecution had failed to prove that the deceased was last seen in the company of the appellant.

facts.fact: There was a major discrepancy between the charge sheet, which alleged a co-accused took the deceased, and the trial testimony of the deceased's wife and brother, who claimed the appellant took the deceased.
facts.evidence: the speciﬁ c allegation that A2 was the one who had taken away the deceased from his house, whereas during deposition the deceased’s wife and his brother have stated that it was the appellant who had taken away the deceased is enough to raise doubts with regard to the veracity and authenticity of such statements.

facts.fact: The prosecution's story was deemed highly improbable, as the deceased allegedly went willingly with the appellant late at night despite a supposed strong animosity between them.
facts.evidence: the fact that the deceased, late at night, agreed to go to the house of the appellant, when seen in the backdrop of the allegation that there was strong animosity between the two, appears to be highly improbable.

facts.fact: The deceased's family did not report him missing for over two days, which cast doubt on their version of events.
facts.evidence: it does not appear that the deceased’s family took any steps to ﬁ nd out as to where the deceased had gone despite being missing for more than two days.

facts.fact: The deceased's wife testified that relations between the parties were cordial, contradicting the prosecution's claim of animosity as a motive.
facts.evidence: The deceased’s wife has testiﬁ ed that relations between the parties were cordial, and has not hinted at animosity.

facts.fact: There was a long time gap between when the deceased was allegedly last seen and when his body was recovered, weakening the 'last seen' theory.
facts.evidence: there is a long time-gap between the alleged last seen and the recovery of the body

facts.fact: The High Court's decision was based on the testimony of a witness (PW10) who had turned hostile during the trial.
facts.evidence: the only material to hold that the deceased was last seen in the company of the appellant, by the High Court, was the testimony of PW10, that too based on the extra-judicial confession by the appellant before the police, when PW10 during trial had turned hostile.

facts.fact: There was a lack of other corroborating evidence, such as forensic proof that the blood found belonged to the deceased.
facts.evidence: in the absence of other corroborative pieces of evidence... most importantly there was no forensic examination conducted to prove that the blood belonged to the deceased.

law.description: The 'last seen' theory can only be invoked when it is proven beyond a reasonable doubt. The mere fact that the accused was last seen with the deceased does not automatically lead to an inference of guilt; there must be additional evidence connecting the accused to the crime.

law.law_name: Burden of Proof in 'Last Seen' Cases
law.description: The onus shifts to the accused to explain what happened to the deceased only after the prosecution has definitively proven with evidence that the deceased was last seen alive in the company of the accused.

In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the chain of circumstances must be complete in all respects, pointing only to the guilt of the accused and excluding any other possible theory of the crime.

When reviewing an acquittal, an appellate court must recognize the double presumption of innocence in favor of the accused. If two views of the evidence are possible, the one favoring the accused must be adopted.

application.step: The Court first determined that the foundational element of the prosecution's case—the 'last seen' theory—was not proven beyond a reasonable doubt.
application.reasoning: This was due to the major discrepancies in witness statements, the improbability of the narrative, and the reliance on a hostile witness (PW10). The Court stated there was 'no deﬁnitive evidence of last seen and that theory itself is in doubt'.

application.step: Since the 'last seen' circumstance was not established, the Court found that the burden of proof did not shift to the appellant to explain the deceased's death.
application.reasoning: The Court distinguished the case from precedents like *Kashi Ram*, stating that in the present case, the very fact of the deceased being with the appellant was not proven, so the appellant had no obligation to provide an explanation.

application.step: The Court evaluated the case as one of circumstantial evidence and found the chain of circumstances to be incomplete.
application.reasoning: The long time-gap, the lack of corroborating forensic evidence, the contradictory testimony regarding motive (animosity vs. cordial relations), and the family's inaction all created significant doubts and broke the chain of evidence, making it unsafe to sustain a conviction.

application.step: Finally, the Court applied the principles of appellate review for an acquittal.
application.reasoning: It held that the High Court erred by overturning the Trial Court's decision. Given the numerous doubts and weaknesses in the prosecution's case, the Trial Court's view acquitting the appellant was a possible and reasonable one. Therefore, the High Court should have upheld the presumption of innocence and sustained the acquittal.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, concluding that it was not justified in reversing the Trial Court's acquittal. The Court found that the prosecution had failed to prove the 'last seen' theory beyond a reasonable doubt due to major discrepancies, improbable circumstances, and a lack of corroborating evidence. As the chain of circumstantial evidence was incomplete, the conviction could not be sustained, and the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the doubt.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal order passed by the Trial Court, which was based on the finding that the prosecution had failed to prove that the deceased was last seen in the company of the appellant.
appellant_arguments: The Trial Court's acquittal was based on cogent evidence and reasons, correctly concluding that the prosecution failed to prove its case.

There was a major contradiction in the prosecution's case: the charge sheet alleged that the co-accused (A2) took the deceased, whereas witnesses (PW3 and PW8) testified in court that it was the appellant who took the deceased.

The burden of proof under Section 106 of the Evidence Act can only shift to the accused if the prosecution first proves with definite evidence that the deceased was last seen with the accused, which it failed to do.
respondent_arguments: Section 106 of the Evidence Act applies where the prosecution has succeeded in proving facts from which a reasonable inference can be drawn regarding the death.
The accused, by virtue of their special knowledge of being last seen with the deceased, must offer an explanation as to what happened.
If the accused, who were last seen with the deceased, withhold information from the court, an inference is justified that they murdered the person.

cases.case_name: Kanhaiya Lal v. State of Rajasthan
cases.principle: For the prosecution to successfully invoke Section 106 of the Evidence Act, they must first establish that there was a fact especially within the knowledge of the accused.

Under Section 106 of the Evidence Act, if a person is last seen with the deceased, the burden is on him to offer a probable and satisfactory explanation as to how and when he parted company with the deceased.

cases.case_name: Ram Gulam Chaudhary v. State of Bihar
cases.principle: Section 106 of the Evidence Act applies where the prosecution has proved facts from which a reasonable inference of death can be drawn, and the accused, who were last seen with the victim, must offer an explanation based on their special knowledge, failing which an adverse inference can be drawn against them.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The burden of proof under Section 106 of the Evidence Act shifts to an accused to offer an explanation only after the prosecution has first succeeded in proving by definite evidence the foundational fact that the deceased was last seen alive in the company of the accused.
obiter: It is ultimately a matter of appreciation of evidence and, therefore, each case must rest on its own facts.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the High Court was not justified in reversing the acquittal because the prosecution failed to prove the foundational fact that the deceased was last seen with the appellant. The burden of proof under Section 106 of the Evidence Act only shifts to the accused after the prosecution has established the 'last seen' circumstance. Since the 'last seen theory' itself was in doubt, the chain of circumstantial evidence was incomplete, making it unsafe to sustain the conviction.
legal_tests_applied: Under Section 106 of the Evidence Act, the burden to offer an explanation shifts to the accused only after the prosecution has first established with definite evidence that the deceased was last seen in their company. As the court stated: 'The burden on the accused would, therefore, kick in, only when the last seen theory is established.'

In cases of acquittal, an appellate court must adhere to the standard that there is a 'double presumption in favour of the accused,' and 'when two views are possible, the one favouring the accused is to be leaned on.'
For a conviction based on circumstantial evidence, the chain of circumstances must be so complete that the only inference that can be drawn is the guilt of the accused.
policy_considerations: The presumption of innocence is a foundational principle, and when doubts arise from the evidence, the benefit must be given to the accused, not the prosecution.
There is a high judicial standard for overturning an acquittal, which includes a 'double presumption' of innocence, to protect individuals from wrongful conviction by an appellate court.
